title: Applied Materials Is About to Post Its First $10 Billion Quarter — and the China Scare Is the Excuse You Should Ignore
subtitle: Record revenue, a $10.25 billion guide, and a China mix that fell from 35% to 28% of sales without losing a single dollar — the AI equipment supercycle is bigger than the narrative.
summary: Applied Materials smashed estimates with record revenue of $9.115 billion and guided to its first-ever $10 billion quarter while raising its WFE growth outlook above 30% — yet the stock sold off on China-mix anxiety before analysts talked it back up. The dip was the story's gift; here's why the supercycle thesis survives the noise.
bodyHtml:
Applied Materials just told Wall Street something it has never said before: it expects a $10 billion quarter. The first $10 billion-plus guide in the company's history — $10.25 billion at the midpoint, up 51% year over year, with earnings guided to $4.02 a share — dropped Thursday night alongside record revenue of $9.115 billion and record non-GAAP EPS of $3.50, both ahead of consensus. The stock still sold off roughly 5% the next day, because a market this addicted to AI growth will always manufacture a worry. That reflex created the exact mispricing this column lives for.

The Numbers That Matter

Market Cap$403B
Forward P/E27.8
Total Revenue (TTM)$30.8B
52-Week Low$154.47
52-Week High$739.67
Analyst ConsensusStrong Buy
Analyst Target Mean$641.03
Price refreshes live · All other figures as of August 17, 2026

The quarter itself was as clean as they come. Revenue of $9.115 billion, up 25% year over year, beat the $8.99 billion consensus; non-GAAP EPS of $3.50, up 41%, topped the $3.40 the Street expected, and GAAP EPS landed at $3.17. For the current quarter the company guides to $10.25 billion at the midpoint, plus or minus $500 million, against a pre-print consensus near $9.5 billion — a guide that is a beat before the quarter even starts. The only flat line was gross margin at roughly 50.4%, and a margin that holds steady while revenue grows 25% is a feature, not a bug.

This is not a company coasting on one good quarter. CEO Gary Dickerson raised the calendar-2026 wafer fab equipment outlook again, now calling for WFE growth above 30%, and peer Lam Research has separately pushed its own 2026 WFE estimate to roughly $150 billion. Advanced packaging — the technology that lets hyperscalers stack more compute into a single package — is growing more than 70% for Applied this year, and the Applied Global Services annuity is compounding above 20%. The AI buildout is becoming a multi-year equipment supercycle, and Applied is the biggest shovel seller in it.

"Another strong growth year" is how management describes 2027, with foundry-logic, DRAM, and advanced packaging combining for roughly 80% of all WFE growth across 2026 and 2027.

Then there is the China question, the real source of the market's anxiety. China accounted for 28% of revenue in the quarter — $2.506 billion — versus 35% a year earlier, and even though the absolute dollars were essentially flat, a falling mix at a forward multiple north of 30 reads like a canary to a nervous tape. Investors spent Friday deciding this was the beginning of the end for Applied's China franchise; management says the opposite, expecting China revenue to grow this calendar year on 28-nanometer foundry-logic demand from fabs that keep buying through every export-control headline. The bear case mistakes mix for momentum.

The tape eventually did what the tape does. Shares fell about 5% the day after the print, rebounded roughly 5.5% on Monday as analysts rushed to defend the story, and Tuesday's broad semiconductor selloff — TSMC, ASML, AMD and friends all in the red — dragged the group down with it. UBS kept its Buy rating while trimming its target from $705 to $675, and the Street's consensus remains a Strong Buy with a mean target near $641 against a range from $358 to $900. That is a wall of analyst support for a company trading at a forward multiple in the high 20s while guiding to 85% EPS growth in the current quarter.

The fundamentals back the enthusiasm. Applied carries net cash of roughly $2.7 billion — $9.2 billion in cash against $6.5 billion in debt — and generated about $3.2 billion in free cash flow over the trailing twelve months, with a $0.53 quarterly dividend going ex-dividend August 20. The trailing P/E near 44 looks rich until you remember the forward multiple in the high 20s applies to earnings growing at a pace the guide just accelerated. Earnings are compounding faster than the multiple, which is the definition of a stock that is cheaper than it looks.

The bottom line is simple: the China-mix scare is a distraction, the flat margin is a non-event, and the only number that matters is a first-ever $10 billion quarter with more growth already booked behind it. Applied Materials is the cleanest way to own the AI equipment supercycle — advanced packaging up 70%, WFE up 30%, a services annuity compounding on top — and the post-earnings dip handed patient buyers a better entry than the story deserved. Own it, add on weakness, and let the multi-year buildout do the work.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in AMAT. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
